notes.bp: A speech system should not degrade one language or gender more than another when audio passes through a codec.
notes.wh: Transcoding changes the signal before recognition or sentiment analysis, and the codec may interact with language and vocal characteristics.
notes.naive: Treat a codec as a neutral pipe and measure only average speech quality.
notes.ap: Transcode millions of multilingual files through PSTN, VoIP, and neural codecs, then compare quality by language and gender.
notes.mech: The study measures speech quality after representative codec paths across more than two million multilingual files.
notes.math: The target is a distribution of quality differences, not one overall mean; grouping by language and gender exposes unequal channel loss.
notes.ww: PSTN codecs show strong gender bias and neural codecs introduce language bias in the reported analysis.
notes.limits: Codec set, languages, gender labels, quality measure, and files define the boundary; causal mechanisms and mitigation in deployed networks remain open.
notes.title: On the Language and Gender Biases in PSTN, VoIP and Neural Audio Codecs

notes.bp: An ASR system should adapt online to an elderly speaker it has not seen, without stopping for a large offline retraining job.
notes.wh: Elderly speakers vary acoustically and linguistically, and one prompt that helps one speaker can hurt another.
notes.naive: Use one speaker-independent model or fine-tune a separate model per speaker.
notes.ap: Cluster speaker prompts into experts and let a router mix acoustic and language prompts for the new speaker at run time.
notes.mech: MOPSA uses K-means speaker prompt clusters and a router around Whisper, with separate acoustic and language-level prompts, tested on English and Cantonese elderly speech.
notes.math: The router is a mixture-of-experts choice; WER/CER measure recognition and real-time factor measures adaptation cost.
notes.ww: The paper reports relative WER/CER reductions of 4.21% and 5.40% and up to 16.12x real-time speedup over offline adaptation.
notes.limits: Datasets, elderly populations, prompt clusters, and Whisper versions bound the claim; broader disorders, languages, and online failure recovery remain open.
notes.title: MOPSA: Mixture of Prompt-Experts Based Speaker Adaptation for Elderly Speech Recognition

notes.bp: A speaker verifier should combine several recognizers while producing scores that mean the same thing across operating thresholds.
notes.wh: Different recognizers make dependent errors and their scores have different scales, so adding scores can miscalibrate decisions.
notes.naive: Use a weighted linear score sum and tune it on one development set.
notes.ap: Model the joint score distribution with flexible marginals and a copula that captures dependency, then fuse and calibrate scores.
notes.mech: Variance-Gamma marginals describe each recognizer's score distribution and a Gaussian copula describes dependence for target and non-target trials.
notes.math: The copula separates marginal shape from dependency; Cllr measures calibration and discrimination of verification scores.
notes.ww: On NIST SRE 2019 and SITW, the method reports up to 7% relative Cllr reduction versus discriminative linear fusion.
notes.limits: Datasets, recognizer diversity, score distributions, and calibration protocol bound the result; new speakers, channels, and attacks need separate evaluation.
notes.title: A Copula-Based Generative Score-Level Fusion Model for Speaker Verification

notes.bp: A listener should be able to see which moments of an audio clip drove a classifier, especially when the model may be using a spurious sound.
notes.wh: There is usually no ground-truth explanation, so explanation methods can look plausible while pointing to the wrong time region.
notes.naive: Trust a saliency plot or compare explanations by visual appeal.
notes.ap: Create time annotations for target events as a proxy reference and benchmark model-agnostic post-hoc explanations against them.
notes.mech: The benchmark compares temporal explanation methods for audio classifiers and uses the annotations to expose spurious correlations.
notes.math: Time-localized overlap turns an explanation into a measurable alignment problem; the proxy is useful but is not a causal proof of model reasoning.
notes.ww: The paper reports near-perfect explanations for some methods and shows their use in finding spurious correlations.
notes.limits: Event annotations, task type, explanation method, and proxy definition bound the claim; faithfulness under distribution shift remains open.
notes.title: Benchmarking Time-localized Explanations for Audio Classification Models

notes.bp: A translation system should translate speech into text for languages with little or no labeled speech data.
notes.wh: Sound-to-meaning transfer crosses languages and modalities, while phonetic evidence is easier to share than complete translated speech examples.
notes.naive: Train a large speech-to-text translator only on languages with parallel speech and translation labels.
notes.ap: Insert phoneme recognition and phoneme-aware chain-of-thought steps, then gradually shift training from text support toward speech.
notes.mech: A multilingual LLM processes speech and phonemes under a curriculum; multilingual benchmarks compare low-, zero-, and high-resource settings.
notes.math: Phonemes form an intermediate representation that can transfer sound structure across languages, while translation quality measures the final meaning transfer.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved low-resource translation and zero-resource operation, with a small high-resource tradeoff.
notes.limits: Languages, phoneme recognizer, curriculum, and benchmark define the boundary; zero-resource claims depend on what other language information is available.
notes.title: Speech-to-Text Translation with Phoneme-Augmented CoT: Enhancing Cross-Lingual Transfer in Low-Resource Scenarios

notes.bp: A person who cannot speak reliably may need a system that turns brain activity into a chosen voice without collecting data from the target speaker first.
notes.wh: EEG is noisy and indirect, while voice identity is highly speaker-specific; conversion must align these signals without target examples.
notes.naive: Train a voice converter only from speech or require target-speaker recordings before conversion.
notes.ap: Align EEG features with speaker voice features and use a speech-trained zero-shot voice-conversion model.
notes.mech: A three-stage training strategy maps EEG to speaker-specific features and conditions a pretrained speech-only converter; Dutch single-word production tests the system.
notes.math: The alignment is a cross-modal mapping problem; zero-shot evaluation tests whether target identity can be supplied without target speech data.
notes.ww: The paper reports reliable target-voice conversion on the Single-Word-Production Dutch-iBIDS dataset.
notes.limits: Single words, EEG setup, target voices, and small dataset define the claim; intelligibility, privacy, consent, and real assistive communication remain open.
notes.title: EEG-based Voice Conversion : Hearing the Voice of Your Brain

notes.bp: A voice assistant should be judged not only by whether it understood a request but also by whether its spoken response sounds natural and conversational.
notes.wh: Semantic accuracy can hide stiff timing, poor prosody, or unpleasant acoustic quality, and existing tests emphasize understanding.
notes.naive: Score a voice assistant with text-task accuracy alone.
notes.ap: Build a benchmark that tests general knowledge, speech recognition/understanding, semantic generation, and acoustic generation together.
notes.mech: SOVA-Bench compares speech LLMs across comprehension and generated-speech dimensions, making acoustic quality an explicit evaluation target.
notes.math: The benchmark separates what the assistant knows, what it understood, and how it sounded; no single score can substitute for those dimensions.
notes.ww: The paper presents a systematic evaluation framework intended to guide speech-LLM voice interaction.
notes.limits: Benchmark tasks, prompts, listeners, model versions, and acoustic measures define the comparison; long-term interaction quality and user adaptation remain open.
notes.title: SOVA-Bench: Benchmarking the Speech Conversation Ability for LLM-based Voice Assistant

notes.bp: A speech-to-speech translator should inherit text-trained language knowledge without needing a huge paired speech-to-speech corpus.
notes.wh: Text-only LLMs know language patterns but not how discrete speech units carry them, and limited paired data makes direct adaptation unstable.
notes.naive: Fine-tune directly on speech units and expect the text model to discover the modality bridge.
notes.ap: Interleave aligned text and speech units during training, then gradually reduce the text proportion so the model moves toward speech output.
notes.mech: LLaMA3.2-1B is fine-tuned on CVSS with scheduled interleaving and evaluated across translation directions and resource levels.
notes.math: The schedule is a curriculum over modalities: text provides a stable scaffold early, while speech units become responsible later; translation quality measures the endpoint.
notes.ww: The paper reports consistent translation improvements, especially in limited-data languages.
notes.limits: CVSS, unitizer, schedule, model size, and languages bound the result; naturalness, speaker identity, and unseen domains need separate tests.
notes.title: Scheduled Interleaved Speech-Text Training for Speech-to-Speech Translation with LLMs
